concepts.name: Article 131: Inter-Governmental Dispute Resolution – Scope and Exclusions
key_dimensions: Exclusive original jurisdiction for disputes between Centre vs State(s) and State vs State involving questions of law or fact
UPSC trap: disputes must involve a 'legal right' – political or non-justiciable disputes are excluded
Exclusion of disputes arising from pre-constitutional treaties, agreements, covenants, or instruments
Comparison with Article 262 (inter-state water disputes) – Article 131 jurisdiction can be ousted by Parliament

concepts.name: Meaning of 'Original Jurisdiction' vs Other Jurisdictions of the Supreme Court
key_dimensions: Distinction between original, appellate, advisory, and writ jurisdiction
Original jurisdiction means SC is the court of first instance – no prior adjudication required
UPSC trap: Writ jurisdiction under Article 32 is also original but distinct from Article 131 original jurisdiction
High Courts also have original jurisdiction (Article 226) – comparison of scope and nature

concepts.name: Locus Standi under Article 131: Who Can Be a Party
key_dimensions: Only the Union of India and State Governments can be parties – not individuals, corporations, or local bodies
UPSC trap: A state government cannot sue on behalf of its citizens or private parties
Union Territory status – UTs are not 'States' under Article 131 and cannot invoke this jurisdiction
Judicial interpretation: State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) clarifying political vs legal disputes

concepts.name: Exclusivity of Supreme Court's Jurisdiction under Article 131
key_dimensions: Article 131 uses the word 'exclusive' – High Courts cannot adjudicate Centre-State disputes of this nature
UPSC trap: Exclusivity does not mean SC has jurisdiction over ALL Centre-State disputes – only those involving legal rights
Parliamentary power to modify exclusivity via legislation (e.g., water disputes under Article 262)
Comparison: Article 131 exclusivity vs non-exclusive original jurisdiction in other matters

concepts.name: Article 131 and Inter-State Water Disputes: Jurisdictional Conflict
key_dimensions: Article 262 empowers Parliament to exclude SC's jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 bars SC jurisdiction – UPSC frequently tests this exception
Recent controversy: States approaching SC despite tribunal mechanism (e.g., Cauvery, Krishna disputes)
SC's ruling in State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu on maintainability under Article 131

concepts.name: Writ Jurisdiction under Article 32 as Original Jurisdiction: Scope and Nature
key_dimensions: Article 32 is a Fundamental Right itself (Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution)
SC can issue five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
UPSC trap: Unlike Article 226 (High Court), Article 32 can ONLY be invoked for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
SC cannot refuse to exercise Article 32 jurisdiction – it is a guaranteed right, not discretionary

concepts.name: Comparison of Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) Writ Jurisdictions
key_dimensions: Article 226 is wider – HC can issue writs for FRs AND 'any other legal right'; Article 32 limited to FRs only
UPSC trap: High Court writs have broader territorial jurisdiction in some contexts but SC writs have pan-India effect
Doctrine of alternative remedy – HC can refuse writ if alternative remedy exists; SC under Article 32 generally cannot
Both jurisdictions are original but SC under Article 32 is a fundamental right, HC under Article 226 is a constitutional right

concepts.name: Five Types of Writs: Scope, Purpose, and UPSC-Tested Distinctions
key_dimensions: Habeas Corpus ('produce the body') – against illegal detention; can be issued against private individuals too
Mandamus ('we command') – cannot be issued against the President/Governor, private individuals, or to enforce a contractual obligation
UPSC trap: Prohibition and Certiorari – both issued against judicial/quasi-judicial bodies but Prohibition is preventive, Certiorari is curative
Quo Warranto – only writ that can be sought by any member of public (not just aggrieved party); applies to public offices

concepts.name: Presidential Election Disputes and Supreme Court's Original Jurisdiction under Article 71
key_dimensions: Article 71 grants SC original jurisdiction to decide disputes relating to election of President and Vice-President
UPSC trap: This is NOT under Article 131 – it is a separate head of original jurisdiction
SC's inquiry is limited to electoral process, not eligibility criteria disputes post-election
Comparison: Election disputes of MPs/MLAs go to High Courts (Article 329), not SC directly

concepts.name: Enforcement of Constitutional Rights vs Statutory Rights: Original Jurisdiction Boundary
key_dimensions: Article 32 writ jurisdiction strictly limited to Fundamental Rights (Part III) – statutory rights must go to HC first
UPSC trap: Directive Principles (Part IV) are NOT enforceable under Article 32 directly
SC's expansive interpretation: linking DPSPs with FRs to expand Article 32 scope (Minerva Mills judgment)
Legal rights under ordinary law cannot be the basis for SC's original writ jurisdiction under Article 32

concepts.name: Original Jurisdiction in Matters Referred by President: Article 143 vs Original Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Article 143 is advisory jurisdiction, NOT original jurisdiction – a common UPSC conceptual trap
SC's opinion under Article 143 is advisory and not binding on the President
Distinction: Original jurisdiction involves adversarial proceedings with binding decisions; advisory is consultative
Instances of Article 143 reference: Ram Janmabhoomi case, Berubari Union case – SC clarified these are advisory

concepts.name: Suits Against the Government: Original Jurisdiction of SC vs Suits in Civil Courts
key_dimensions: Article 131 does not cover all suits by/against government – ordinary civil suits go to regular civil courts
Government of India Act, 1935 legacy: federal court had original jurisdiction which was inherited by SC
UPSC trap: A private party cannot invoke Article 131 even if suing the government – jurisdiction is exclusively inter-governmental
Contrast with US Supreme Court's original jurisdiction which includes suits by foreign diplomats and admiralty cases

concepts.name: Doctrine of 'Legal Right' Requirement in Article 131 Disputes
key_dimensions: SC has held disputes must involve a legally enforceable right, not merely a political grievance
State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977): SC ruled that political disputes over dissolution of assemblies are not covered
UPSC trap: A state's disagreement with a central policy (e.g., GST rates) does not automatically qualify under Article 131
Recent example: Kerala's suit against the Citizenship Amendment Act – SC examined maintainability under Article 131

concepts.name: Parliamentary Legislation Ousting Supreme Court's Original Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Article 131 proviso: Parliament can by law confer jurisdiction on SC with respect to matters in Union List – but can also oust
Article 262: Parliament excluded SC's jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes – key UPSC tested example
UPSC trap: Parliament cannot oust SC's jurisdiction under Article 32 (it is a Fundamental Right) – but can limit Article 131
Judicial review of parliamentary exclusion of SC jurisdiction – Basic Structure doctrine as a limit

concepts.name: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) as an Extension of Original Writ Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: PIL is a judicial innovation expanding Article 32 – relaxed locus standi to allow any public-spirited citizen to approach SC
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981): SC liberalized standing; Hussainara Khatoon case (undertrial prisoners) as early PIL
UPSC trap: PIL is not a separate jurisdiction – it operates within Article 32 original writ jurisdiction
SC's own guidelines to prevent PIL misuse (2010 guidelines); distinction between genuine PIL and personal interest litigation

concepts.name: Territorial Scope of Supreme Court Writs vs High Court Writs
key_dimensions: SC writs under Article 32 operate throughout the territory of India – pan-India enforcement
HC writs under Article 226 generally limited to territorial jurisdiction of the HC concerned
UPSC trap: A HC can issue writs against authorities outside its territory if the cause of action partly arises within its jurisdiction
Practical implication: SC is preferred for matters involving multiple states or central government authorities

concepts.name: Original Jurisdiction vs Transferred Cases: Article 139A
key_dimensions: Article 139A empowers SC to transfer cases involving the same/substantially similar questions of law from HCs to itself
UPSC trap: This transfer jurisdiction is NOT the same as original jurisdiction – SC is not a court of first instance here
SC can also transfer criminal or civil cases from one HC/court to another under Article 142 and CPC/CrPC powers
Distinction between Article 131 (true original), Article 32 (original writ), and Article 139A (transfer/consolidation)

concepts.name: Remedies Available under Article 32: Beyond Writs
key_dimensions: Article 32(1) guarantees the right to move SC for enforcement of FRs – not limited only to writs
Article 32(2): SC may issue 'directions, orders, or writs' – broader than just five traditional writs
SC has used this to create new remedies: compensation for violation of FRs (Rudul Shah case, 1983)
UPSC trap: SC can award monetary compensation under Article 32 for constitutional tort – not just in civil suits

concepts.name: Recent Controversies in Article 131 Jurisdiction: Contemporary Cases
key_dimensions: Kerala v. Union of India (CAA challenge, 2020): First instance of a state filing suit under Article 131 against central legislation
Debate: Can states challenge constitutional validity of central laws under Article 131 or must they use Article 32/226?
SC's preliminary examination of maintainability: whether the dispute involves 'legal right' of the state qua state
Implication for federalism: Article 131 as a tool for states to resist central encroachment on state subjects

concepts.name: Comparison of India's Supreme Court Original Jurisdiction with Other Federal Democracies
key_dimensions: USA: Supreme Court has original jurisdiction over disputes between states and cases involving ambassadors – broader in some respects
Australia: High Court has original jurisdiction similar to India's Article 131 for inter-governmental disputes
UPSC angle: India's SC original jurisdiction is more restricted than USA – Indian SC's main strength is appellate and writ jurisdiction
India's SC lacks admiralty and prize jurisdiction as original jurisdiction unlike some other federal courts
